To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Fe- or Mo-induced Cu deficiency in cows and their calves is associated with reduced plasma Cu concentrations and cerulo-plasmin activities, and that these changes are associated with reduced growth rates of Mo-supplemented calves.

1) feeding diets high in iron and molybendum (Mo) can cause Cu deficiency in beef cows and calves and 2) feeding a Cu-supplemented diet to beef cows during the last one-third to one-half of gestation and throughout the lactation period will prevent Cu deficiency in the calves.

1) dietary Cu depletion caused by feeding diets high either in Fe or Mo resulted in decreased plasma Cu and cerulopasmin activity in beef cows and calves; and 2) calves from cows fed diets high in Fe or Mo had reduced growth rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of Cu deficiency on growth performance and Cu status in beef cows and calves, with a special focus on the role of Fe and Mo in Cu metabolism.
the effects of copper depletion by feeding diets with high levels of iron or molyb-denum on performance and copper status of cows and calves.
the role of copper (Cu), iron (Fe) and molyb-denum (Mo) in ruminant nutrition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the addition of 5 to 10 mg of Mo/kg to the diet of beef cows and their calves did not adversely affect growth performance of calves or Cu status of cows or calves.
the addition of 600 mg Fe/kg or 10 mg Cu/kg to the diet had no effect on the growth or Cu status of beef calves.
the study demonstrated the effects of copper depletion by feeding diets with high levels of iron and molybendum on performance and copper status of cattle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Cu supplementation of beef cows and their calves can prevent Cu deficiency, and that the addition of Fe to the cow diet will not exacerbate Cu status of the calves.
copper depletion can be caused by either iron or molybde-num supplementation of the diet.
copper is important for beef cows and calves in the last trimester of pregnancy and the first 4 months of life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of copper to the diets of beef cows and their offspring can help maintain copper status and growth performance.
the effects of Fe and Mo on Cu status of cattle are dependent on the dietary Cu concentration and are not additive.
copper supplementation in the diet of beef heifers entering the last one third of gestation will improve the copper status of their calves at birth and through weaning.
